prompt.brief: Design a distributed cache like Redis or Memcached that serves key-value reads and writes with predictable low latency, bounded memory, replication, and recovery.
successSignals: Define key ownership, TTL behavior, eviction policy, and the consistency contract for reads, writes, and deletes.
Use partitioning and hot-key isolation to serve 10M operations per second over a 1TB working set without a single-node bottleneck.
Separate cache operations from replication, rebalancing, eviction telemetry, and warmup so background work cannot stall requests.
Explain node failure, quorum or primary-replica choices, cache stampede protection, security, and degraded behavior.

functional: Store, retrieve, overwrite, and delete values by namespace and key.
Support per-entry TTL, explicit expiration, and an observable miss or expired result.
Provide atomic compare-and-set and increment operations for callers that need coordination.
Distribute entries across cache nodes and replicate selected partitions for failure recovery.
Expose node, partition, memory, eviction, and replication health to operators.
Allow authenticated clients to use namespaces, quotas, and encryption in transit.
nonFunctional: Keep the normal GET, SET, and DELETE path below p99 5ms inside a region.
Handle 10M cache operations per second and a 1TB working set with horizontal partitioning.
Keep a node failure from losing acknowledged writes beyond the declared durability contract.
Bound memory, queue depth, replication lag, and recovery work so overload is visible and controlled.
Degrade predictably during a partition, backing-store failure, or hot-key event.
scaleAssumptions: Serve 10M operations per second at peak over approximately 1TB of active values.
Assume a roughly 90:10 read-to-write ratio, with a small set of keys capable of becoming extremely hot.
Partition by a hash of namespace and key; keep replicas in separate failure zones and reserve headroom for rebalancing.
Treat the cache as the serving layer unless the product explicitly requires durable writes to a backing database.

metrics.label: Peak throughput
metrics.description: Capacity assumption that drives shard count, connection limits, and backpressure.

metrics.label: Working set
metrics.description: Memory and replica capacity must include metadata, fragmentation, and failover headroom.

metrics.label: Operation latency
metrics.description: Budget for the regional cache path, excluding optional asynchronous telemetry.

metrics.label: Replica freshness
metrics.description: Operational target for asynchronous replicas when the chosen consistency mode permits it.

metrics.label: Cache effectiveness
metrics.value: >= 95% hit rate for hot working set
metrics.description: A product-specific target that must be measured by namespace and key class, not only globally.

entities.name: CacheEntry
entities.notes: The serving record returned by a cache read. Version and expiry travel with the value so stale replicas and expired entries can be rejected.

entities.name: CacheNode
entities.notes: A cache process or shard host that owns partitions and reports capacity, health, and membership state.

entities.name: Partition
entities.notes: The routing and failover unit. Its epoch prevents an old owner from accepting writes after rebalancing.

entities.name: Replica
entities.notes: Replication state for a partition copy, including whether it can be promoted and how far it has caught up.

entities.name: EvictionRecord
entities.notes: Bounded telemetry for TTL and memory-pressure evictions; it is not part of the cache read critical path.

apis.contract: { consistency?, version? } -> { hit, value?, version, expiresAt?, servedBy }
apis.notes: Route the key to its current owner, return a hit or miss, and apply the requested consistency mode without reading an unrelated control-plane resource.

apis.contract: { value, ttlSeconds?, expectedVersion?, writeMode } -> { version, expiresAt, replicationStatus }
apis.notes: Write at the partition primary with an atomic version check, then acknowledge according to the configured primary-only or replica-quorum contract.
Write a tombstone or deletion version through the same partition owner so a delayed replica cannot resurrect the value.
Bound batch size and preserve per-key partition ordering; never turn a batch into unbounded synchronous fan-out.

apis.contract: { nodes[], partitions[], hitRate, evictionRate, replicationLag, freshness }
apis.notes: Return operational health and freshness separately from data reads so clients do not mistake a healthy cache process for a fresh replica.

dataFlow.title: Route the key to a partition
dataFlow.description: The gateway authenticates the namespace, hashes namespace plus key, and uses a versioned partition map to select the primary or an eligible replica.

dataFlow.title: Serve a cache hit
dataFlow.description: The cache node checks the entry version and expiresAt in memory, returns the value immediately, and increments bounded local hit telemetry.

dataFlow.title: Read or write the primary
dataFlow.description: A miss reads the current partition owner and fills the local entry; a SET, DELETE, or atomic operation updates the primary with a conditional version check.

dataFlow.title: Replicate the partition change
dataFlow.description: The primary appends the mutation to a per-partition replication log and acknowledges after the selected consistency boundary, while replicas apply mutations in order.

dataFlow.title: Evict, rebalance, and recover asynchronously
dataFlow.description: Background workers expire or evict entries, move hash ranges, warm replicas, and promote a caught-up copy after failure without blocking healthy cache operations.

architecture.title: Distributed Cache reference architecture
architecture.summary: A partitioned in-memory serving tier handles the key-value critical path, while a membership store, replication log, and bounded background workers handle consistency, eviction, rebalancing, and recovery. The cache contract makes durability and stale-read behavior explicit instead of treating every cache as an implicit database.

layers.label: Client and request edge
layers.description: Authenticated clients enter through a bounded API boundary that applies namespace policy and rate limits.

layers.label: Partitioned serving tier
layers.description: Routing and cache nodes serve reads and writes from memory with per-partition ownership.

layers.label: Membership and replication
layers.description: The partition map and replication log provide epochs, ordered mutations, and recovery evidence.

layers.label: Async maintenance
layers.description: Eviction, rebalancing, warmup, and repair remain bounded background work.

layers.label: Reliability operations
layers.description: Operators can see latency, hit rate, memory pressure, hot keys, and replica freshness.

keyPaths.label: Cache operation path
keyPaths.description: Client -> gateway -> router -> cache cluster, with the membership store supplying the partition map.

keyPaths.label: Replication path
keyPaths.description: Cache cluster -> replication log -> cache replicas, with ordered offsets and a declared acknowledgement policy.

keyPaths.label: Maintenance and recovery path
keyPaths.description: Monitoring -> maintenance and warmup workers -> partitioned cache cluster for eviction, movement, and repair.

components.label: Application clients
components.description: Services use GET, SET, DELETE, and atomic cache operations with namespace credentials.

properties.traffic: Reads, writes, invalidations, and bounded batches

components.label: Cache API gateway
components.description: Authenticates namespaces, validates payload size and TTL, applies quotas, and bounds request fan-out.

properties.protection: mTLS or tokens, quotas, payload limits, and abuse controls

components.label: Partition router
components.description: Hashes namespace and key, caches the partition map, and routes to an owner using the current epoch.

properties.strategy: Consistent hashing or fixed hash slots with epoch-aware ownership

components.label: Partitioned cache cluster
components.description: In-memory primaries and replicas execute bounded key operations, enforce TTL, and maintain per-partition versions.

properties.capacity: 1TB working set plus replica and failover headroom
properties.hotKeys: Request coalescing, replication, and per-key protection

components.label: Membership and partition store
components.description: Stores node membership, hash ranges, epochs, replica assignments, namespace policy, and recovery state.

properties.consistency: Quorum or strongly consistent updates for ownership changes

components.label: Partition replication log
components.description: Carries ordered mutations and checkpoints so replicas can catch up, be audited, or be rebuilt.

properties.delivery: At least once with offset deduplication

components.label: Eviction and rebalance workers
components.description: Apply TTL cleanup, LRU or LFU policy, partition movement, throttled repair, and failure promotion.

properties.safety: Bounded concurrency, leases, epochs, and resumable checkpoints

components.label: Replica warmup workers
components.description: Preload selected keys after movement or promotion without allowing warmup traffic to starve foreground requests.

properties.backpressure: Priority and rate limits per namespace and partition

components.label: Cache reliability monitoring
components.description: Tracks p99 latency, hit rate, memory pressure, evictions, hot keys, ownership churn, and replica lag.

properties.signals: SLOs, saturation, freshness, failovers, and namespace-level quotas

connections.label: Validate and route
connections.description: The gateway passes a bounded operation to the partition router.

connections.label: GET / SET / DELETE
connections.description: The router sends the operation to the current partition owner.

connections.label: Partition map
connections.description: The router refreshes ownership and epoch metadata when its local map is stale.

connections.label: Ownership heartbeat
connections.description: Nodes publish health and ownership acknowledgements for failover decisions.

connections.label: Ordered mutations
connections.description: Primary mutations enter the per-partition replication stream after validation.

connections.label: Offsets and repair
connections.description: Workers consume mutation offsets and repair or promote replicas.

connections.label: Evict or rebalance
connections.description: Maintenance changes are throttled and checked against the current ownership epoch.

connections.label: Warmup jobs
connections.description: Selected keys are scheduled for bounded preloading after movement or promotion.

connections.label: Throttled preload
connections.description: Warmup restores hot data without taking priority over foreground operations.

connections.label: Latency and freshness
connections.description: Nodes emit bounded metrics for SLOs, saturation, hit rate, and replica lag.

deepDives.title: Partitioning and consistent hashing
points: Hash namespace plus key into fixed slots or a consistent-hash ring so adding a node moves a bounded fraction of entries.
Keep the partition map versioned. A request carrying an old epoch must refresh or fail rather than write to a previous owner.
Use virtual nodes or fixed slots to spread uneven key sizes, and reserve capacity for a node or zone failure.

deepDives.title: Replication and consistency
points: Primary-replica replication is simple for ordered writes; quorum acknowledgements improve durability but add latency and reduce availability during a partition.
Offer an explicit consistency mode such as primary, session, or quorum read instead of hiding stale-read behavior in the client library.
Replicate deletes as versioned tombstones so delayed data cannot resurrect after expiry or invalidation.

deepDives.title: TTL, eviction, and memory pressure
points: Enforce expiresAt on reads even if lazy cleanup has not run; background TTL scans are storage maintenance, not correctness.
Choose LRU, LFU, or a sampled hybrid based on workload, and reserve memory for metadata, replication buffers, and fragmentation.
Expose eviction reason and namespace so a hit-rate drop is distinguishable from an origin or routing failure.

deepDives.title: Hot keys and cache stampedes
points: A balanced hash ring does not prevent one viral key from overloading its owner; replicate hot entries and coalesce concurrent misses.
Use jittered TTLs, request collapsing, stale-while-revalidate where allowed, and per-key rate limits to avoid synchronized expiry.
Do not let warmup or repair consume the same connection and CPU budget as foreground requests.

deepDives.title: Failure recovery and rebalancing
points: Use leases, heartbeats, and fencing epochs to decide when a replica can be promoted and to prevent split-brain owners.
Rebalance gradually with per-partition checkpoints, admission control, and rollback or pause points.
After a failover, mark freshness and missing ranges explicitly; do not claim that a cache hit is durable data unless the contract says so.

deepDives.title: Durability boundary
points: If the cache is only a derived layer, a miss can reload from the backing store; if it is the source of truth, acknowledged writes need a durable log or replicated storage.
Keep the product decision visible in the API and metrics because it changes whether node loss is a cache miss or data loss.
Backups and snapshots should be asynchronous and rate-limited so they do not consume the foreground latency budget.

deepDives.title: Security and multi-tenancy
points: Authenticate clients, isolate namespaces, enforce maximum value size and TTL, and prevent one tenant from exhausting memory or connections.
Encrypt traffic between clients and nodes, and avoid placing secrets or regulated data in a cache without an explicit retention policy.
Audit administrative flush, failover, and topology operations separately from high-volume data operations.

deepDives.title: Degraded operation
points: When a replica is stale, return a miss or a clearly bounded stale value according to the namespace contract; never silently turn a correctness-sensitive read into arbitrary stale data.
Use circuit breakers and bounded retries for unavailable nodes, and protect the backing store from a miss storm.
Alert on partition unavailability, replica lag, and origin load before the global cache hit rate makes the problem obvious.

tradeoffs.title: Cache-aside versus write-through
tradeoffs.recommendation: Use cache-aside when the backing store owns durability and write-through when a shared cache abstraction must coordinate writes consistently.
tradeoffs.caution: Cache-aside can create stampedes and stale entries; write-through couples cache availability and write latency to the backing store.

tradeoffs.title: Primary-replica versus quorum replication
tradeoffs.recommendation: Start with primary-replica ordering and a documented acknowledgement mode; add quorum only for namespaces that need stronger durability or read guarantees.
tradeoffs.caution: Quorum improves failure semantics but consumes latency and availability budget during network partitions.

tradeoffs.title: Fixed slots versus a hash ring
tradeoffs.recommendation: Use fixed hash slots for predictable ownership and tooling, or a consistent-hash ring when incremental node movement is the dominant concern.
tradeoffs.caution: Both need hot-key isolation, versioned membership, and a migration strategy; the hashing algorithm alone is not a rebalancing plan.

tradeoffs.title: LRU versus LFU eviction
tradeoffs.recommendation: Use LRU for recency-heavy workloads and LFU or a sampled hybrid when long-lived popular keys should survive bursts of one-time traffic.
tradeoffs.caution: An eviction policy can optimize memory but cannot repair a bad TTL, oversized value, or hot-key distribution.

tradeoffs.title: Stale reads versus fail-closed reads
tradeoffs.recommendation: Choose per namespace: tolerate bounded stale data for feeds and metadata, but fail closed or reload from an authority for authorization and inventory decisions.
tradeoffs.caution: A global fail-open or fail-closed policy makes unrelated workloads absorb each other’s failure semantics.

commonMistakes: Treating a cache as durable storage without defining how acknowledged writes survive node and zone loss.
Using a hash ring without versioned ownership, fencing, rebalancing checkpoints, or hot-key protection.
Checking TTL only in a background cleanup job, which allows expired values to be served between scans.
Allowing synchronized expiry, uncoordinated misses, or warmup traffic to create a backing-store stampede.
Reporting only global hit rate while hiding namespace memory pressure, eviction reason, partition skew, and replica lag.
Retrying indefinitely on a failed node and turning a local cache outage into a larger dependency outage.

followUps.question: What happens when a cache node fails during a write?
followUps.answer: Return success only after the configured acknowledgement boundary, use the partition epoch to promote an eligible replica, and reconcile uncertain writes from the replication log or backing store before retrying.

followUps.question: How do you prevent one hot key from taking down a shard?
followUps.answer: Detect per-key skew, replicate or locally duplicate the hot value, coalesce misses, and apply per-key protection without moving every ordinary key or adding synchronous fan-out.

followUps.question: How do you rebalance without a long outage?
followUps.answer: Move partitions incrementally with a new ownership epoch, copy or stream data to the destination, fence the old owner, and switch traffic only after the destination is ready.

followUps.question: Is a stale value acceptable during an outage?
followUps.answer: Make it a namespace-level contract. Serve only bounded stale data for tolerant consumers, and fail closed or consult the authoritative store for correctness-sensitive decisions.

rubric.description: The answer states throughput, working set, latency, read/write mix, TTL, hit-rate, and durability assumptions that drive the design.
The answer makes CacheEntry, partition ownership, node membership, replica state, versions, and hot-key access patterns explicit.
The answer explains acknowledgement modes, stale reads, tombstones, epochs, promotion, rebalancing, and degraded behavior.
The answer covers eviction, TTL enforcement, stampede protection, hot keys, bounded background work, and per-namespace isolation.
The answer ties monitoring to cache SLOs and can defend the choices between cache-aside, replication, partitioning, eviction, and stale-read policies.
